The purpose of this research was to examine the decay process of certain particles called $B^0_s$ into two other particles, $K^+$ and $K^-$, and to determine the natural time frame for this process. To do this, researchers first needed to measure the rate at which these particles become aligned in the same direction, a phenomenon known as coherence. To achieve this, they combined the results from previous experiments to obtain a more accurate understanding, and then compared it to the time it takes for the two particles to fall out of sync with each other due to their differing energies. By doing so, they were able to establish that the time frame for this process is significantly longer than current observational limits, and therefore, current experiments have the capability to consistently detect these particles even when they are not coherent. Furthermore, this finding has implications for a specific theoretical prediction related to certain particle interactions, and by using this result, the necessary conditions can be established to make certain experiments sensitive to this prediction.

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a controlled diffusion equation with random initial conditions. The study presents a theoretical analysis of the error between the exact solution and a numerical solution obtained using a finite element method on a continuous time grid. Specifically, the paper establishes a new error estimate when the underlying PDE includes a random parameter. This investigation provides an alternative error bound compared to existing literature.

A comprehensive analysis of cosmic-ray data at extremely high energies has been presented in a comprehensive study of x-ray flares from supermassive black holes.  The study used comprehensive datasets from the Pierre Auger Observatory and MAGIC telescopes to demonstrate the likelihood of observing large-scale fluctuations in cosmic-rays and x-ray flares simultaneously.  By accounting for potential magnetic distortions in cosmic-rays, the study found a significant increase in likely occurrences of such simultaneous observations, to over 3 times more probable than not, given the extreme conditions of these events.  The study also used total energy released in x-ray flares to predict the density of cosmic-rays and found a significant discrepancy, to over 5 times more probable than not, given the large size of these events. The assessments of mid-rapidity proton and particle spectra, as well as nuclear alteration factors in p+Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV using p+p collision data at 5.02 TeV and 7 TeV have been performed by the ATLAS collaboration. Measured quantities include mid-rapidity proton and particle spectra, nuclear alteration factors for proton spectra, and the altitude factor for identified particles. Additionally, the assessment of the collision energy in p+Pb collisions has been validated using rescaled p+p data.

This paper explores the connection between quantum mechanics on noncommutative phase space and its associated Lie algebra. We examine the deformation of a harmonic oscillator based on a su(2) algebra and then extend this to a higher-dimensional algebra, specifically boc(2). Additionally, we discuss the challenges of developing a quantum mechanical framework on a noncommutative torus space that accurately reflects the geometry of its algebraic foundation.

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze medical images at multiple institutions. The goal was to classify tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) in whole-slide images, which is critical in understanding the interaction between cancer and the immune system. We compared the results of training a convolutional neural network using both federated learning and a centralized approach. Although the models yielded similar accuracy, the federated learning method offered advantages in data protection and the ability to update the model without consolidating the images. This proof-of-concept study highlights the potential of federated learning in developing more accurate and generalizable models for categorizing medical images.

In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a seawater test cable that incorporates 12 nearby water immersion fibers.  Compensation techniques for chromatic dispersion and the effects of water on the fiber are incorporated into the transmission system.  Experimental measurements show that, following the application of these techniques through real-time digital signal processing, the performance of the transmission system remains superior even in the presence of burst errors resulting from the variation of water conditions along the length of the fiber.  The enhancement in performance is attributed to the training-based optimization of equalization settings that takes into account the unique characteristics of the seawater environment and the physical properties of the fiber.  The validity of the transmission system is confirmed through 24 hours of continuous testing at a data rate of 72Gbit/s.  The characteristics of the seawater environment and the physical properties of the fiber continue to vary over time, causing the system to experience burst errors at irregular intervals.  Nevertheless, the incorporation of real-time digital signal processing and the training-based optimization of equalization settings enable the system to maintain a high level of performance even in the presence of these complications.

Temporal convolutional networks have gained popularity in forecasting tasks due to their flexibility and efficiency, but they require significant computational resources. The high parameter count of TCN arises from the extensive use of persistent connections and recurrent architecture, which poses a challenge in network optimization. To overcome this limitation, a novel framework called Trimming In Time (PIT) has been developed to efficiently train TCN by reducing unnecessary connection weights. The PIT framework is designed to balance the trade-off between preserving the temporal dynamics of the data and eliminating redundant weights. It achieves this balance through an adaptive learning algorithm that identifies and optimizes temporal pattern coefficients automatically. The benefits of PIT are twofold: it facilitates the use of high-performance optimizers like Adam by transforming TCN into a standard fully connected network, and it enables the direct application of filter techniques such as thresholding and cumulative sum. The performance of PIT is evaluated on real-world datasets, demonstrating its capacity to rival state-of-the-art methods while reducing training time and model parameters substantially.

This paper proves that any variety of linear algebras in general form, which includes nilpotent algebras, solvable algebras, and their respective varieties, characteristically nilpotent algebras, as well as their solvable counterparts, characteristically solvable algebras, has the property of being solvable or nilpotent in nature. Furthermore, this achievement yields the specific outcome that any variety of the so-called Zinbiel algebras, which are distinctive linear algebras defined by a particular law, will inevitably be solvable or nilpotent.

Our study offers initial evidence for charge-neutral particle emissions aligned with a flow direction in Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. A specific angle, denoted as $\psi$, is determined through two methods, and fluctuations in particle yield and flow intensity are quantified in dependance on this angle, revealing an evident rise in fluctuations at an optimal angle of approximately $0.4$ times satellite angle $\Delta\psi$. As the optimal angle varies between experiments, our findings are further validated by theoretical models, such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and DREISER, which predict similar fluctuations in initial state and final state, respectively.

The unified correspondence theory is a key framework in modeling various parallel extension programs, notably including grid programs, answer set programs with functional and equality constraints, and programs for instance validation. The unified correspondence theory demonstrates the equivalence between the solutions produced by these programs and the models formed through the interpretation of a specific class of modal logics, known as DLE-logics, in a particular framework. While significant work has been completed in establishing the correspondence between specific DLE-logics and program types, a comprehensive approach has yet to be developed. In contrast, our research proposes a novel, more general method for establishing the correspondence between any program of a certain category and its DLE-logic, leveraging this approach to also provide evidence for the universal validity of a particular statement.

Information tables containing missing values and functional relationships between certain data fields are addressed in this research. We establish a new concept of functional nullness for functional dependencies, stating that if a value satisfies a dependency, all entries with the same underlying value must also satisfy the same dependency. Based on this principle, we develop a notation for functional nulls that maintains data integrity and allows for consistent inference. We further prove that certain combinations of functional nulls and missing values are inherently incompatibile. These discrepancies cannot be resolved by simply filling in missing values or eliminating certain nulls. In contrast, certain pairs of nulls and missing values are compatible and may be handled by filling in specific values. We introduce algorithms for identifying and managing compatible discrepancies, including determining the minimum number of values that need to be known in order to resolve the discrepancies and the specific values that need to be filled in. Our approach may be viewed as an extension to the conventional theory of relations, incorporating handling of missing values and functional relationships.

This study presents a novel temporal-variance Poisson autoregressive model, which incorporates an exponential function to adapt count data dependencies to changing patterns. The new model builds upon existing PARS models, leveraging a rich historical dataset to estimate varying count relationships. Estimation is achieved through maximum likelihood optimization, and a robust check has been established to ensure the model's stability. A simulation test has validated the accuracy of the proposed method, while a real-world crime data analysis reveals the benefits of using the new model.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates the success of neural networks in image recognition tasks using object
descriptors and poses. NDFs are designed to be invariant to transformations and
tensors that can be learned from end-to-end using pose annotations. During training, NDFs use a multi-view approach that utilizes both 2D and 3D object descriptors to minimize pose estimation errors. In testing, the NDF is used to predict object poses and identify misclassified objects. Experiments demonstrate that NDFs can replicate classification performance based on pose annotations alone and outperform SE(3)-agnostic object classification networks. The code for NDFs is available at https://github.com/gualtiero.prato/Neural-Descriptor-Fields.

The SiD (Scanning Detector) collider detector for the ILC (International Linear Collider) has been thoroughly assessed in its existing form, and the review has led to a revised design that maintains its superior performance while reducing costs. The revised SiD detector preserves its exceptional all-around performance, achieving accurate momentum measurement and versatile particle identification, alongside excellent energy and momentum resolution. The revised design demonstrates that the original SiD goals can be achieved with a 20% cost reduction, using the same 3D calorimeter and scintillator detector design that maintains low material content and high efficiency. The revised forward pixel detector increases forward particle tracking efficiency without increasing the overall cost.

We performed external exposure measurements on five rich stellar clusters in the Milky Way using the spectrograph on the Blanco 4m telescope. The data were collected as part of the Bulge Cluster APOGEY project and were observed under decent to excellent seeing conditions, with most observations taken with a $R$-band filter. The measurements for Tonantzintla 2 were compared to previous findings, showing a solar-type cluster distance of 3.79 kiloparsecs, a metal content of -0.07 times the sun's metal content, and a cluster age of 600 million years. The cluster's absolute $M_V$ magnitude of -8.35 was determined, and its luminosity function matched earlier findings by Gómez and Chávez (2004). A Luminosity Function Model was used to analyze the data, and the results for Tonantzintla 2 were contrasted with those of three other open clusters studied with the same technique, particularly the double galaxy cluster TC 2.

The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed a vast collection of proofs over the years, offering a rich source for research in theorem verification. Despite the numerous opportunities presented, little work has been done to date on comprehensive analyses of this archive. Our project undertakes an in-depth examination of Isabelle theories, involving the exploration of theorem interconnections, verification checkers, and documentation content. To facilitate future collaboration, we are releasing our analysis results in an enhanced form for the benefit of the Isabelle community.

Using the functional renormalization group at the edge of integration, we have analyzed the Yang-Lee edge singularity in classical O(N) universality classes. By comparing the bare propagators before the edge to their renormalized counterparts at the edge, we established a universal relationship that enables the determination of critical exponents without explicit access to the edge. This relationship led to a previously overlooked criterion for universality that surpasses the conventional framework. Applying this approach to the universality classes at hand, we found that the edge singularity in the Ising model is already maximally broadened when the mass parameter reaches the renormalized mass at the edge, located at $\Gamma_{\text{edge}}=2e^2/\hbar v$. Similarly, for the O(N) universality classes with $N\neq 2$, the edge singularity is as broadened as the disordered phase's widest point, and this occurs when the renormalized mass at the edge is given by $\Gamma_{\text{edge}}=2(N+1)e^2/\hbar v$. Notably, this result specifically contradicts a previous prediction made by Chandra et al.

In statistics and machine learning, the approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm has been effectively applied to solve various inverse problems by developing an efficient and scalable method for minimizing the Bethe free energy. However, the accuracy of its results relies on the validation of a specific inequality derived from a minimization problem with convex constraints. Despite the success of AMP in real-world applications, a rigorous justification of its results has remained a missing link in the literature. Recently, a team of researchers developed an innovative approach that provides an explicit expression for the subgradient of a specific function in an efficient way. This new strategy enables the application of convex optimization tools, thereby enabling a rigorous analysis of the accuracy of AMP in solving various inverse problems. In an independent line of research, a novel expression for the TAP free energy was previously obtained through an extensive computational algebra. In this study, the authors combine the strengths of both approaches by deriving a concise expression for its second-order partial derivatives. This achievement relies on an intricate mixture of computational algebra, matrix factorization, and the application of convex optimization tools. The authors demonstrate that the TAP free energy exhibits a local concave property, which may have far-reaching implications in the field.

Modern wireless communications are experiencing exponential growth, yet the availability of spectrum is limited, making frequency band utilization extremely precious. To optimize performance, it is essential to control wave propagation characteristics at the microscale, allowing for precise manipulation of propagation properties at the macroscale. This control can be achieved through the deliberate design of photonic structures, specifically metasurfaces, which are constructed from repeated electric field responsive components and can operate at multiple frequency bands simultaneously. This paper proposes a holistic approach to modeling metasurfaces, incorporating their geometric structure, physical properties, and interactive electromagnetic mechanisms to create a unified framework. By leveraging this approach, it becomes possible to investigate the electromagnetic properties of complex structures like metasurfaces, enabling the study of frequency-dependent interactions between electromagnetic waves and these structures. To further illustrate the capabilities of this approach, a comprehensive analysis of a binary-amplitude mosaic metasurface in operation at 60 GHz is conducted, considering the effects of material anisotropy and lossy components to evaluate its robustness and authenticity.

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for smooth fully integrable vector fields on areas of higher dimensionality. The key hypothesis relies on the existence of a neighborhood around the origin, within which the vector field in question can be converted into a linear combination of vector fields with eigenvalues zero through a diffeomorphism that is smoothly compatible with the original vector field's invariant manifold. In order to prove this conclusion, the study first establishes that local smooth orbital linearization is an automatic consequence of the global smooth orbital linearization theorem. Next, the research focuses on demonstrating that the smooth fully integrable vector field can be linearized locally and smoothly within its associated invariant manifold by utilizing a combination of the global linearization theorem and local techniques. Additionally, it is shown that linearization can be achieved using a smooth change of variables that is explicitly defined in terms of the local inverse of the global linearization map, particularly within the context of dimension two.

This study proposes a deep learning approach to accurately predict multi-electron interactions within complex systems, leveraging a simplified potential energy surface based on coupled channels. In this method, artificial neural networks specifically designed for potential energy function approximation are used to predict the remaining electron interactions after a limited number of electrons have been accurately described. Our model simplifies the challenging problem of many-electron physics by dividing the electron cohort into two distinct groups: those whose behavior is thoroughly understood, and those whose behavior needs to be predicted. Through a key experiment involving two experimental configurations, our proposed strategy is compared to more conventional methods of prediction. Furthermore, our model's capability to predict the energy levels of nitrogen molecule anions is also examined. The results of these experiments demonstrate that our proposed strategy not only surpasses the performance of control models, but also matches the accuracy of established methods of prediction.

Researchers discovered a massive curve-like structure in the distribution of galaxies at a high altitude in the sky using the Sloan Digital Sky Map. Unlike the Milky Way and its neighboring galaxies, which form a flat disk, this region features a curved shape resembling a ring. A massive spiral arm within the Milky Way may be reflected in the observed pattern of galaxy clustering. In contrast, most models of galaxy clustering fail to notice the curved feature. A simple model that incorporates a reflection symmetry in the Milky Way's spiral arm is able to explain the observed galaxy clustering in the northern high-altitude region. This finding may have implications for the detection of galaxy clustering in the southern hemisphere.

While using photometry from low-cost devices, several challenges need to be addressed, including the requirement for multiple simultaneous observations of at least three photometric bands. This paper explores the utilization of photometry from a single device, specifically aiming to determine the aerosol content in the atmosphere. We examine two methods: one based on the use of specific wavelengths (wavelength method) and another utilizing the entire spectral range (integral method). The study employs data from a specific device and incorporates two different atmospheric models, as well as data from 365 satellites operating in orbit around the Earth. The results show that the wavelength method yields the most accurate readings when using data from the satellite, while the integral method performs better when using the device. Furthermore, we investigate the optimal wavelength for the wavelength method and find that the choice of system parameters, such as the Scanning Rate, has an impact on the accuracy of the aerosol assessment. The study also compares the aerosol content calculated from photometry and collected from ground-based stations, revealing a correlation but also highlighting the limitations of the technique. The study concludes by outlining potential avenues for research, including the need to create low-cost multiband photometry devices and integrating the method with machine learning algorithms.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping in the initial stage and correspondence learning in the subsequent stage. We initially employ a patch-based method to generate virtual control points and then develop a simple but robust method to solve the projection grouping problem to derive the intrinsic object parameters. A convolutional classifier is then utilized to generate the relative coordinates of points on the object with respect to a fixed reference point, and the absolute coordinates are subsequently obtained through a simple addition operation. The 2D-3D correspondence problem is formulated as a classification task, and a point-wise confidence score is introduced to filter unreliable correspondences. A robust set of correspondences is selectively obtained through a classification-based priority system. The pose RANSAC algorithm is modified to incorporate the confidence score to obtain an accurate and stable pose estimate. The proposed framework, known as DeepHMap++, is evaluated using five datasets, and the results show a significant improvement over the existing state-of-the-art methods.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuity formation within materials. Bond-based Peridynamics has gained particular interest for its precise capture of material fracture by developing non-overlapping fragments. Initially developed for solid mechanics, researchers have begun adapting BB-PD to model fluid dynamics, addressing topics such as free surface flows and boundary conditions. This paper delves into the implications of non-local interactions in fluid mechanics, exploring how considerations of finite particle size, of the order of nanometres to millimetres, affect our understanding of fluids. It also investigates how BB-PD's distinctive PD kernel affects both local and non-local interactions with fluids, examining various kernel properties and their effects on model behaviour. Ultimately, the study suggests that choosing PD kernels carefully is crucial, as it can lead to consistent models that integrate well with boundary conditions and other physical principles, and potentially even offer a more robust framework for modeling real-world fluids that defy ideal fluid assumptions.

We present GGLasso, a Python-based library designed to address Generalized Graphical Lasso (GGL) challenges. This includes solving complex inverse problems by determining the inverse of a parameter matrix influencing changes in an output matrix, while assuming these relationships follow a known stochastic process. Furthermore, GGLasso supports estimating these inverse matrices using Lasso regression and Graphical Lasso algorithms.

Numerous analysis techniques and molecular modeling methods rely on sampling configurations, which are fundamental to understanding and characterizing molecular systems. Metropolis Integration of Molecular Dynamics into Force Fields, a highly efficient sampling approach, integrates MD trajectories into FFs to achieve systematic coverage of configuration space. However, its application is limited to metabolically compatible systems. In contrast, simple thermodynamic integration of MD simulations into FFs is more versatile and can be applied to any system. This method integrates the FF force field into the thermodynamic perturbation framework to evaluate property averages, which are then calculated as a function of the integration parameter. This study enhances the simplicity and efficiency of this approach by incorporating multiple MD trajectories obtained at different temperatures, allowing the calculation of properties as a function of temperature. This method is supported by an open-source Python package called pidy, which provides a user-friendly and efficient framework for combining MD simulations into FFs.

Numerical relativity is utilized to examine how gravitational waves generated by merging black holes are affected by the presence of dark energy. Although a cosmological constant is thought to comprise approximately 68% of the universe's energy density, its effect on gravitational waves is expected to be minimal due to the large scale of the wave's amplitude. Yet, the precision required for future detectors such as LISA in the next decade of research will necessitate a thorough understanding of this impact. The 1+log type of transition used in previous studies is replaced by a more accurate 1+2 interface in the latest research, allowing for a more precise analysis of the interaction's impact on the gravitational wave spectrum. The adoption of this interface is motivated by the desire to increase the accuracy of waveform templates, with the goal of directly observing dark energy through the interaction's effect on gravitational waves rather than other parameters. The results of this study demonstrate that the 1+2 interface leads to a more precise calculation of the energy density of gravitational waves and potentially their amplitude, particularly in the high frequency range. The study also reveals that the behavior of the wave spectrum is influenced by the ENSR ratio characteristic of the interface, with values ranging from approximately 1 to 5. The effect of the interface on wave spectra is predicted to be significant enough to be detectable with the aid of future detectors in specific scenarios.

We investigate the stability of an Euler-Bernoulli beam residing on a star-shaped metric space and discuss how it relates to a phenomenon where two infinitely long, aligned beams, experiencing a specific type of external pressure, become subject to a certain boundary condition at their combined point.

Researchers utilized silicon carbonates with varying carbon content as novel acoustic lenses with different absorption properties for a multi-spectral PA system. By adjusting the carbon amount, four different silicon carbonates were created with distinct optical and PA characteristics. Experiments demonstrated that lenses made from these materials could effectively direct different frequency PA waves. Various configurations of these lenses were also tested to increase the detection area covered by the PA system. The performance of a single lens and a pair of lenses was evaluated and their effectiveness as acoustic lenses proved. However, using multiple lenses may distort photoacoustic signals. Furthermore, increasing the carbon content in silicon carbonates was found to decrease their mechanical strength. Therefore, it is crucial to strike a balance between the acoustic properties and the robustness of these materials.

The concept of prominence in network analysis has been widely applied across various disciplines to identify highly connected nodes and sensitive network components. Initially developed for single-layer networks, recent advancements enable the study of prominence in multilayer networks, where nodes have distinct connections and significance levels across different layers. In this paper, a novel approach is introduced to determine prominence in multilayer networks, where the significance of each node is linked to its connectivity within each layer. By combining the altered Raggio and Grasedel methods, a computationally efficient framework is established to handle layer-wise dependence. The introduced approach is demonstrated through applications to a multilayer air transportation network and a co-authorship network.

We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on noisy raw images using a novel approach that leverages a collaborative learning strategy. By assuming that an unknown operator connects demosaicking and deblurring processes, we develop a three-player game involving pointwise and integral operators. To solve this, we apply a hybrid method that incorporates both alternating minimization and closed-form solution techniques. Our approach yields an efficient algorithm that utilizes mainly first-order methods and can function with limited and noise-corrupted training data. Notably, our algorithm achieves highly competitive performance on several benchmark datasets while requiring significantly fewer training samples.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture.

The Causal Learning category has seen substantial growth in recent years, with numerous methods developed to address complex problems. However, evaluating and interpreting these methods is increasingly challenging due to limited data availability for causal analysis. As a result, researchers often rely on synthetic data generated by causal mechanisms, but they lack a unified framework to assess the performance of their models in capturing these mechanisms. To address this need, we present the Causal Exploration Toolbox, a comprehensive suite of tools designed to evaluate and compare causal models using various metrics and visualization techniques. This framework enables researchers to enhance the explanatory capabilities of their models by identifying latent causal relationships within their output, as demonstrated through its application to Causal Neural Network Ensembles.

Research has long been conducted to study the seal performance of spheres in various fluid environments, and multiple models have been proposed to explain sealing action. However, these models often lack a key factor: the role of surface tension in the flow. Additionally, previous studies have primarily focused on high-speed scenarios, neglecting the dynamics of spheres moving at intermediate speeds through different fluids. This study explores the interaction between a sphere and a less dense fluid at speeds where which surface tension has a significant impact, by investigating how it affects the sphere's sealing behavior and flow pattern. Experiments were conducted with spheres entering into water at speeds ranging from 0cm/s to 20m/s, and various factors including surface tension, sphere size, and minor impurities on the sphere surface were examined. The results revealed that surface tension plays a crucial role in the sphere's sealing performance and flow pattern, and had a notable impact even at the highest speed tested. A new model is also presented, incorporating surface tension to explain the sphere's sealing behavior and flow pattern. This model distinguishes between three regimes defined by changes in surface tension and sphere speed, and includes a novel "cap" model for low-speed regimes. This study's findings and model can be applied to better understand and predict the sealing performance of spheres in various fluid environments moving at intermediate speeds.

A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Our research indicates that the extension of alpha'-corrections in the effective field theories is key, as it results in the emergence of novel theta-terms associated with global symmetries in the field theories. Specifically, we demonstrated that the range of universal symmetries potentially present is determined by the range in which the novel theta-terms are made exact by the alpha'-corrections. Our findings also suggest that the range of universal symmetries may be narrowed down to T-duality, as the novel theta-terms associated with other global symmetries can be made exact by incorporating higher derivative corrections linked to the self-duality of the Type IIB graviton multiplet.

APIs hold valuable information, but to protect them, an expensive and time-consuming process is undertaken to identify and fix vulnerabilities. A novel approach is being proposed, one that utilizes an unusual hardware-based technique to circumvent privacy policies and deliver malicious code, thereby accelerating the discovery of API weaknesses. Instead of hijacking user sessions or tricking individuals into installing malicious software, this method leverages a unique hardware exploit that bypasses security measures and allows for the rapid identification of API vulnerabilities. The success of this technique is demonstrated through its application to discovering vulnerabilities in real-world APIs, including those governed by strict privacy policies. The development of APIs that are resistant to this type of hardware-based exploitation is also explored as a means of mitigating its effects.

We investigated the challenges of offline policy evaluation and optimization in dynamic environments, particularly the significant issues that arise when a significant portion of data is inaccurate. In scenarios where a substantial percentage of observations are flawed, conventional methods like value iteration networks and batch policy evaluation fail, resulting in inaccurate estimates. We discovered that a significant portion of this difficulty stems from the fact that environment changes affect notifications about action outcomes, leading to corrupted data that affects notifications about action outcomes, resulting in corrupted data that further impacts estimates. To address this challenge, we proposed a quantitative measurement of the impact of corruption on estimates and employed it to evaluate the effectiveness of various methods in scenarios involving severe data corruption. Our research involves collecting a new set of datasets that include corrupted data and conducts comprehensive experiments to demonstrate the superiority of direct objective estimation over indirect estimation using value function approximation. Our findings show that in scenarios involving severe data corruption, the performance of reinforcement learning methods can vary based on the density of the dataset and the structure of the action probability model. To achieve the best results, it is crucial to select a starting model that is carefully randomized and gradually refine it through the removal of corrupt data and reinforcement learning. Our research finds that removing the most corrupt data or the most confident observations results in the best performance.

We uncover an intriguing paradox in the selectionless box game, a thought experiment involving observation effects. The scenario presents a seemingly inescapable consequence - that the player's knowledge must always lead to an unambiguous outcome, whereas quantum mechanics suggests a lack of certainty until actual observation. Our analysis shows that this paradoxical result arises from an unrealistic assumption and yields a more harmonious integration of the player's knowledge and quantum mechanics. Additionally, we explore the implications of this solution for the shape of the particle's wave function and find that certain features of the player's knowledge can be reconciled with the neutral box game scenario.

Investigating cupricite CuFe2S3, we have found that the electronic properties of this 3d transition metal compound exhibit unusual features to withstand high pressures and temperatures inherent to deep-seated ore formations. Using a combination of theoretical and experimental techniques, we uncovered the intricate orbital selection behavior in this substance, specifically highlighting the prevalence of correlations between electron orbits. Our findings reveal the distinct energies at which electrons may occupy various orbital paths and how they are affected by pressure. Under high-pressure conditions, the increase in certain orbital energies while decreasing others leads to an irregular shaping of the orbital paths as the crystal structure undergoes strain. Our research also identifies the unique, pressure-induced movements of electrons as they transition between different states and how they are modulated by the presence of strong interactions between electrons.

In combined quantum systems, superexchange interactions facilitate the pairing of dissimilar objects like spin and charge. This interaction is usually activated by an external magnetic field. Researchers have discovered a novel strategy to activate this pairing without external magnetic field by leveraging a phenomenon called Dicke explosion. This approach involves creating a highly entangled state of atoms or photons through a laser pulse, which results in massive Rabi oscillations in coupled systems in their vacuum state. Utilizing a potential-free exciton as a non-equilibrium state in a nanowire and interface materials, scientists have found a way to observe this phenomenon directly. By employing optical spectroscopy, they have successfully demonstrated massive Rabi oscillations in these systems.

Our investigation reveals that a two-dimensional lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper structure can give adjustable Dirac points within a specific energy band. This band is isolated from other energy bands by sizable gaps. The Dirac points in this context are unique because their locations can be modified through lattice distortions within specific constraints. This property makes them resistant to vacuum external influences. As a result, we propose that this structure's surface could be suitable for producing semi-metallic materials with adjustable energy spectra.

We investigate a scenario where an arbitrary number of coherent light signals can generate multi-phonon coherent states in an optical cavity. A key factor in this process is a single-photon detector that, in response to detecting a photon, releases a specific amount of fuel, represented as a cat state in an auxiliary mode. This catalytic process allows for the creation of multi-phonon coherent states via quantum reflection of the cat state, mediated by the interaction between the light signals and the auxiliary mode. To achieve this, we consider three distinct scenarios based on the type of fuel provided. Furthermore, we show that, with the provision of sufficient fuel, it is possible to create a coherent state with a high amplitude in a cavity initially occupied by a vacuum state. This phenomenon raises the question of whether it is possible to create a state with an arbitrarily large amplitude. To address this, we propose a proposal for detecting multi-phonon coherent states based on the formation of photon-number correlations in a secondary cavity. Our research finds that the state prepared through the catalytic process matches the expected multi-phonon coherent state when the photon number is even, but does not match when the photon number is odd. Consequently, we can use the detection of photon number correlations in the secondary cavity to distinguish between even and odd photon numbers.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, research on electromagnetism's properties has led to identifying comprehensive sets of stable solutions within the context of GR. This study expands on previous findings by exhaustively compiling Weyl's complete set of matrix solutions, matching those of electromagnetism, in the Newman-Penrose framework.

A new technique for developing sequence-based predictions of polymer properties is introduced, allowing multiple types of polymers to be analyzed through the use of indicator variables. This technique combines linear regression with combinatorial optimization to predict properties of individual sequences and aggregate predictions for entire families of polymers. The method enables the incorporation of sequence-based features and has been applied to three public datasets, yielding results that outperform existing models.

This study focuses on addressing lung infection transmission between patients in a hospital setting using a novel approach to dual-patient virtual reality simulation. The goal is to develop software that can rapidly test the effectiveness of various breathing patterns for reducing aerosol transmission between patients. The program uses a complex system dynamics model, incorporating various phenomena such as particle diffusion, heat transfer, and flow patterns, to simulate the transmission of infectious droplets produced by coughing and breathing. The model incorporates multiple variables that can be manipulated through a range of controls, including the frequency and depth of breathing, coughing intensity, head position, and the use of a face shield. The software uses direct transcription to solve the resulting nonlinear optimal control problem, converting the problem into a continuous time-based system and solving it through Newton-Raphson method. The program includes a unique feature called the optimal reaching impulse, which allows a specific breathing pattern to be achieved through control, and this feature is utilized in the case study presented. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of breathing exercises derived from the software in reducing the transmission of infectious droplets through aerosols, and these results highlight the potential of the software to contribute to finding solutions to pressing healthcare issues.

Identifying esophageal tumors from CT scans is a critical procedure for cancer diagnosis and treatment planning. However, medical professionals' accuracy is hindered by the intricacy of CT images and limited field of view during endoscopy, which often results in tumors being detected at an advanced stage. One method to overcome this constraint is the development of automated segmentation systems for early tumor detection during CT scans. Such a system can alert medical professionals to areas with neoplasms, enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of tumor identification. Presently available dense unet-based models primarily focus on pairwise connection between input and output features, which can lead to decreased performance by neglecting lateral connections between intermediate features. Inspired by recent proposals on attention and dense connections, we introduce a new architecture called dilated dense attention unet, which is characterized by three key components: spatial attention, dense connections, and adjustable dilated convolutions. This architecture allows for reduced computation cost and increased flexibility by only conveying significant spatial information from the input signal and combining it with more robust feature representations obtained from intermediate layers. Our model comprises 14 layers, 4 dense layers with 1024, 512, 256, and 128 units respectively, and employs pre-trained weights from the pre-trained unet. We conducted numerous experiments with this model, and the results demonstrated its superior performance in comparison to conventional unets by achieving a mean diameter ratio of 0.16, mean surface ratio of 0.19, and mean DSC

The geosteering technique is utilized for optimal oil recovery by allowing real-time well placement decisions. To support this process, engineers need access to accurate and up-to-date information about the subsurface. This can be obtained through the analysis of collective well data, which includes reviews of previous wells along with current observations from the drilling location. By combining static and dynamic data from nearby wells, engineers can create models that predict the properties of the surrounding formation. These predictions are made dynamically as more well data becomes available, and can be modified to account for uncertainties. By utilizing Bayesian methods, the assessments of uncertainty can be updated as more information from the well becomes available. As a result, engineers can create probability models that reflect their current understanding of the subsurface, enabling them to make informed decisions about well placement in real-time.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling.

We examine a specific class of curves – those that are part of a tropical quartic surface – in order to change their definition from "tropical" to "algebraic". By using this approach, we are able to count the number of curves in this class that intersect another curve exactly once, a task that would be more complicated using traditional algebraic methods. Our method is also fast enough to handle very large sets of these curves. We can count not just the total number of curves but also how they are arranged in space and the order in which they appear when we move from one point to another. This is a notable achievement because many of these curves do not have a clear or "rational" expression in terms of other geometric shapes, which makes counting them difficult. We can count not just the total number of curves but also how they are arranged in space and the order in which they appear when we move from one point to another. This is a notable achievement because many of these curves do not have a clear or "rational" expression in terms of other geometric shapes, which makes counting them difficult. Our method also allows us to look at these curves in pairs, which gives us additional information about their shapes.

Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative algorithm suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks, capable of withstanding interference between different technologies. By utilizing a method where a mobile node sends single-bit information to multiple sensors, we achieve higher accuracy by selecting the maximum number of sensors that receive the information correctly. Our results show that our proposed approach, combined with existing techniques, can yield the most precise results in scenarios affected by CRTD.

Code-mixed languages involve the combination of two or more languages within a single writing system, presenting a distinct challenge for NLP techniques that are typically tailored to solo languages. While research has made progress in this area, numerous obstacles remain, affecting the effectiveness of current methods and limiting their applicability to communities that do use code-mixed languages. To date, most studies have focused on two combinations of languages: English with other languages and Hindi with English, with relatively few experiments conducted on other code-mixed pairs. Furthermore, research has largely ignored the practical implications of code-mixed models for users from diverse cultural backgrounds. In contrast, people from multilingual communities regularly use different languages in social media posts, blending together at least two languages quite frequently. Consequently, there is significant potential for these users to benefit from code-mixed NLP tools. However, to fully realize this potential, NLP systems need to be designed to handle the varied syntax, semantics, and vocabulary associated with multiple languages. Therefore, it is essential to explore alternative models that can seamlessly integrate the features of several languages, enabling them to perform tasks such as classification, sentiment analysis, and text generation more effectively.

Human references are typically used to evaluate image description models by indicating the accuracy of generated captions. Most current studies rely on crowdsourced data but have limitations, as they don't utilize actual human references for comparison. Our research utilizes both crowdsourced and automated annotation sources to evaluate the effectiveness of existing evaluation metrics for descriptive models. By utilizing actual human references, we utilize different annotation sources to analyze the influence of crowdsourcing on evaluation outcomes. Crowdsourcing findings show that current evaluation metrics perform reasonably well when comparing the quality of descriptive models using actual human references as standards. Furthermore, we find that crowdsourcing and automated annotation sources produce similar outcomes, as both reveal that current evaluation metrics are sufficient for ranking descriptive models.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, have been extensively investigated for their exceptional electrical, mechanical, and optical properties.  Recent theoretical studies suggested that Ta$_2$O$_5$ could exhibit metallic properties, going against its commonly accepted insulating nature.  To resolve this contradiction, researchers need to determine the fundamental crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$.  Combining ab-initio and Monte Carlo simulations, our study finds that Ta$_2$O$_5$ settles into a stable metallic state with a bcc structure, matching experimental findings.  Our results also demonstrate that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s electrical properties are highly dependent on crystal size, with smaller sizes exhibiting semiconducting characteristics.  Our findings are consistent with experimental data collected using X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, resistivity, and SEM analysis.  Additionally, our study includes a discussion on the effects of varying oxygen vacancies and a proposed model for Ta$_2$O$_5$ electron energy loss spectrum.  Our results provide a comprehensive understanding of Ta$_2$O$_5$'s electrical properties and suggest that researchers consider factors such as crystal size, oxygen content, and vacuum level when interpreting experimental data.

The concept of the Big Sort, a term coined by David Karber and Barbara Friedman, suggests that Americans are dividing geographically by political affiliations and are only socializing with like-minded individuals. This separation of social circles may contribute to the spread of false information due to reduced exposure to opposing viewpoints. Our research examines the extent of misinformation dissemination among Reddit users in the United States, focusing on how the Big Sort affects it. We analyzed 1800 Reddit posters whose comments were rated as false, and compared them to a random sample of 1800 users whose comments were rated as true, using measures such as density of social connections and user location. Our results show that users who post false information have fewer connected friends and are more likely to live in areas where there is a high concentration of like-minded individuals; these factors contribute significantly to the spread of false information. Furthermore, reducing social connections and slowing down geographical sorting may decrease the dissemination of false information.

We investigate the challenge of detecting anomalous events in real-time, high-speed information flows. Our proposed approach, centered around stochastic process models, enables the simultaneous tracking and prediction of future developments. By comparing observed outcomes to forecasted probabilities, a scoring system is established to identify unusual occurrences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through numerical experiments and its practical applications in various settings, including statistical process control, information system security, and financial market analysis. Furthermore, we examine the potential benefits of integrating contextual information into the model and present an approach to handling multiple information flows simultaneously.

Instructors use spoken language to guide students in various tasks, supplying essential feedback that helps refine their performance and advance in skill level. As robotic learning technology advances, understanding the impact of human instructors is now critical. Research has already demonstrated that human feedback via speech aids robotic learning by increasing training efficiency and speed. To fully leverage the benefits of human instruction, it is essential to understand how speech patterns influence the development of robotic skills. This study examines speech made by human instructors while they demonstrate manipulation tasks to a robotic learner. First, our findings reveal that the speech used is more accurate in describing intended actions than actual actions taken by the robot. Second, the speech used correlates strongly with the skills developed by the robot, while the actual actions taken by the robot are less consistent with the instructions given. Third, our research shows that the instructions given by humans influence the skills developed by the robot in a flexible and indirect manner, with speech serving as a reliable metric for evaluating this process.

Building on previous work, we propose a novel algorithm to randomly generate ordered trees of any degree, based on a pre-specified sequence of numbers representing possible node connections. Our method allows for the generation of binary, n-ary trees, or those with various connection patterns. We demonstrate that this algorithm is both accurate and efficient, running in O(n) time with 'n' representing the number of desired nodes. Additionally, we explore potential applications of the algorithm, illustrating its use in deriving formulas by utilizing the underlying proof of correctness.

A special class of field theories, characterized by Euler-Arnold equations, is explored in this study, focusing on their fundamental properties and the unique solutions they enable, particularly in two-dimensional spacetime. The existing knowledge on Euler-Arnold equations is reviewed, and our mathematical framework reveals that these equations are capable of describing rigid body motions, generating symmetries in spacetime, and deriving simple solution forms through separation of variables. The relationship between Euler-Arnold equations and Liouville field theories is also revealed, and our analysis shows that these equations can be formulated in a broad category of spacetime dimensions, thereby offering a universal theoretical framework.

The growing presence of conversational bots in society necessitates a more thorough understanding of their functionality and potential misfunctions. As a result, industry standards for bot testing have emerged, covering aspects from usability to operational performance. Against this backdrop, German standards for testing chatbots are now integrated with existing methods, now part of a broader testing framework that addresses multiple types of conversational interfaces. This integration is the result of collaborative efforts between German standards organizations and international experts in chatbot research. As a key achievement, this merged framework includes a wide-ranging set of test cases for both command-based and conversational bots, spanning areas like input validation, system integration, and scenario testing. Additionally, the adoption of contemporary concepts of testing, such as model-based testing and model checking, expands the possibilities for bot testing. Furthermore, open-source tools and techniques are now available to implement this testing framework.

The hypothetical Planet X is a concept based on the idea that there may be an undiscovered celestial body influencing the motion of the known planets in our solar system. To support this theory, researchers have analyzed the existing data on the orbital patterns of the planets and found statistical evidence in two separate studies. However, an independent verification of this theory would require observing the gravitational effect of Planet X on the planets directly. Unfortunately, due to the significant mass of the planets themselves, their orbital patterns override any signature that Planet X might have on their movement, making it impossible to confirm the existence of Planet X through this method. Consequently, we have undertaken a new approach to verify the existence of Planet X by focusing on the gravitational influence it would have on the orbital patterns of the inner planets, specifically Earth and Mars. In our analysis, we utilized the existing data on the positions of these planets in our solar system and applied a statistical method to identify any patterns that could be attributed to the gravitational effect of an unseen planet. Our findings for Earth show no significant evidence of this gravitational impact, but our analysis for Mars reveals a slight effect at a 97.5% confidence level, equivalent to a mass for Planet X of approximately 10 times the mass of the Earth. Notably, this analysis is only relevant to the orbital patterns of the inner planets and does not take into account their orbital periods, which would provide a much stricter 99.9% confidence level for a 5 Earth mass Planet X.
